The real question is, why don't they just kill everybody who's seen it and lock it in a box? This implies that somebody above Level 1 has looked at it, either to study it or during a breach, but if that the case it must've happened after the 682 test. It definitely indicates that no civilians have seen it.

Or, alternative theory, they keep it under observation because they're afraid it'll try to kill 682 again, thus supplying a very hostile anomaly with what could be a very dangerous weapon.

Tests have established that this effect is not operative on non-humans

Apparently, the Foundation knows that 682 is human, or else they wouldn't have even tried the termination. 231-4 confirmed?

item.title: I have a bit of a joke experiment I'd like to propose
item.content:encoded:
So, here's what we do so we can allow direct observers to survive a lot longer while containing SCP-689 so we don't have to go through so many D-class. We tape the SCP to the inside of a large helmet and have one observer wear the helmet, with the only possible thing for the observer to see, being the SCP, no matter how close or blurry it will appear, it will still technically be in sight. The helmet will be irremovable, unless a key is present. In order to keep it from killing observers in their sleep, we simply unlock it, and switch it off to another designated observer. Thus allowing shifts. While observers will still be restricted to the containment chamber, this should dramatically increase their lifespans during testing, and allow for testing periods of much longer degrees.

I know its a dumb and irrelevant bit of input, but I just think it's kinda funny to imagine some bloke wearing a giant helmet having to stare at the very lethal SCP all day.

Everyone's pointed it out already, but I'll mention it to.

There is no possible way that someone is too important for immediate termination, but not important enough to be killed in the event of a containment breach. If you're on a list that requires you to be killed at any moment, then there is no difference to killing them you or killing you later. If you're so important that at any time your death may be required without prejudice, then you're better off dead now. Know what I'm saying? It's been stated that the thing prefers to go to populated areas, and know that when there's no one left to kill it stays there. This means that at some point, the Foundation has managed to expose enough people to this fucking statue that a massive kill list is required. Send in the blind people with their covers and put the thing in a room. It will stay there, everything will be good.

This thing feels like the Foundation have systematically managed to fuck everything up beyond repair. Shove this thing in a safe, kill everyone associated with it, and ignore it. item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm surprised that no one's mentioned this before. The containment procedures fall into the "The Foundation is full of idiots" section. Several people have observed that "Why don't we just store it away and *not look at it*" The response has been: "Well, we assume … " that someone looked at the skip and they're being protected.

First problem: They know what happens when the skip has no one on it's kill list. This means they had it at a safe state at one point in time, experimented with it in a safe state, and then exposed people to it.

Second problem: The containment procedures involve 'Try to kill everyone on this list within 10 seconds.' but they have not *yet* implemented the remote kill switch, because the containment procedures are merely 'recommending' the remote kill switches. WHY DO THEY NOT HAVE REMOTE KILL SWITCHES YET?

Third problem: The containment procedures for a power outage involve trying to kill all SCP personnel who are on its kill list. If there was any civilian exposure at all (most popular theory), this would ENSURE a major containment breach because it would have no choice but to reappear within a civilian population. To give the foundation credit, we can simply take this as proof that there is no civilian targets on the skip's kill list.

Therefore, we can determine that only Foundation personnel are on its kill list. The personnel which are slated to be killed within ten seconds of a power failure. So they can't be that important. They're risking a minor breach, and to have valuable Foundation personnel on its kill list … why?

The article doesn't say. We're all making assumptions, so let's assume there's 1 person in the facility important enough to be risking O5 personnel on. Someone they're willing to kill within ten seconds if the power goes out, but too important to kill to keep them from accidentally getting an O5 personnel or any other valuable L4 or L3 personnel from getting put on the kill list.

If there was some such theoretical valuable employee they were protecting by keeping this thing active …

WHY ARE THEY NOT IN THE CONTAINMENT PROCEDURES.

At the very least, they need to hang a sign around their neck going "By being in the same room as me you're risking death" along with a set of pamphlets that everyone who is around them needs to read just to know SCP-689's security procedures of "If you see a green statue on my chest and I'm dead, you're already dead, too. STARE AT THE STATUE. Do not look away or someone else will die as well." AND the containment procedures need to have an expiration date of "When █████████ dies, all other individuals who have seen SCP-689 will be scheduled for immediate termination, and the containment procedures will be altered to be to put this thing in a box and then weld that box shut so no one ever looks at it again."

With appropriate clinical tone, of course.

"If SCP-689 is known to have left the chamber at any time, retrieval teams consisting of blind or visored personnel equipped with echolocators along with Class D observers must be dispatched to the location of all personnel who have previously viewed SCP-689."

Furthermore, this line among others implies that the current containment failure procedures are effective, or that they have a complete grasp on those who have seen it, and that they are all personnel.

If there are others that have seen it that the Foundation doesn't know about, then this wouldn't "ensure that the object does not escape containment."

If what you say was true, the SCP would be scary, but the document just isn't consistent with that idea.

item.content:encoded:
I personally chalk it up to the difference between something that we know is something else and regularly exhibits behavior consistent with being that something else, and something looking like a familiar object and acting for all purposes consistently with that object.

For example, one could say that SCP-1850 appears to be a "full-size 1917 Sopwith Triplane aircraft", because although it looks like a plane, it exhibits behavior consistent with that of a bird but is not actually a bird. It has plane parts analogous to bird parts, though. SCP-1468 are Chickadees, and although they may be some abomination disguised as cute little birdies, they generally exhibit behavior consistent with that of Chickadees (save for the carving).

Basically, if you say that "SCP-XXXX is something", then the reader has a better idea of what sort of general behavior or characteristics to inherently attribute to the SCP without the article needing to state it (Chickadees eat and sleep and defecate and fly around because they're birds and birds do that, and the article doesn't need to state the reasons why it would be disconcerting if birds are starving themselves which is because they're birds and they need to eat otherwise they'll die). Using "appears" leaves the reader in considerably more narrative dark.
